phonemes.desc: Mu plus short epsilon — the name begins with a soft, warning sound.
Delta plus diphthong ου — the middle syllable that carries the hissing.
Sigma plus short alpha — the final hiss that ends the name like a snake's warning.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MEH-doh-sah' — stress the first syllable, as the Greek acute marks; the middle ου is a long closed 'o' [oː] (a spurious diphthong), not 'oo'.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *med- 'to measure, to judge, to guard' — root of Greek μέδεσθαι and Latin mederi

kin.label: Gorgon
kin.form: One of the three Gorgons; her sisters are Stheno and Euryale

pronunciation.note: Médousa is Tier 1 because the Greek Μέδουσα carries both stress (the acute on the first syllable) and a long vowel (the diphthong ου). The name means 'Guardian' or 'Queen,' an ironic title for a figure whose gaze turns men to stone.

domains.title: The Gorgon
domains.subtitle: Petrification, Monsters, Death, and the Averted Gaze
domains.lead: Médousa is the most famous monster in Greek myth — the only mortal Gorgon, whose gaze turns the living to stone. Once, in the Roman telling, she was a beautiful maiden; in the earlier Greek sources she was never anything but horror. She is the danger of the seen that cannot be looked at directly — and the power that heroes must confront through mirrors and shields.

cards.name: The Petrifying Gaze
cards.desc: To look directly at her is to become stone — the literal freezing of fear.

cards.name: Snake-Haired Horror
cards.desc: Her hair is a writhing mass of serpents, the uncanny made visible.

cards.name: The Decapitated Head
cards.desc: Perseus cut off her head; Athena placed it on her aegis as an apotropaic weapon.

cards.name: Birth from Blood
cards.desc: From her severed neck sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor — death producing wonder.

symbols.name: Snakes

symbols.name: Pegasus

mythology.lead: Médousa's myth is unusual because it has a before and an after — and the Greek and Roman sources tell those halves differently. She was the mortal sister among three Gorgons; she was beheaded while asleep, and her blood bore winged horses; and her severed face became the most widely traveled apotropaic image of the ancient world.

myths.title: The Three Gorgons
myths.text: Hesiod gives the Gorgons' genealogy in the Theogony (270–283): they are daughters of the sea-deities Phorcys and Ceto, sisters of the Graeae, and they dwell beyond the stream of Ocean at the world's edge, near the gardens of the Hesperides. There were three: Sthenno, Euryale, and Médousa — and of the three 'only she was mortal.' Pindar remembers the hissing grief of the sisters (Pythian 12.9–12), the sound Perseus heard as he flew away with the head. In the archaic Greek imagination Médousa was never a maiden wronged; she was born a monster, one of a triad of border-horrors guarding the far edge of the mapped world. Her mortality is the myth's hinge: the gods can afford to send a hero against her precisely because, alone of her kind, she can die. The Greeks made the Gorgons the daughters of the old sea — monsters belong to the deep past, the generation before the gods took charge.

myths.title: From Maiden to Monster
myths.text: The famous transformation story is Roman, not Greek. Ovid tells it in the Metamorphoses (4.790–803): Médousa was once a maiden of surpassing beauty, famed above all for her hair — and Neptune lay with her in the temple of Minerva. The goddess averted her virgin eyes and punished the desecration by transforming the mortal's glorious hair into foul snakes. No earlier Greek author knows this story: Hesiod has no rape, no punishment, no metamorphosis, and Apollodorus follows the older line. The discrepancy is the point. Ovid's version makes Médousa a victim twice over — of the god who used her and of the goddess who blamed her — and turns the snake-hair from a birth-trait into a sentence. Roman readers wept for her; Greek votaries flinched from her. The same face carries both meanings, and every later age has chosen which one to see.

myths.title: Perseus and the Head
myths.text: Polydectes, king of Seriphos, sent Perseus to fetch the Gorgon's head, expecting him never to return. The gods equipped the impossible errand: Athena lent her polished shield, Hermês the adamantine sickle (harpe) — in some accounts forged by Hephaistos — Hades the cap of invisibility, the nymphs the kibisis-bag and winged sandals. Perseus first forced directions from the Graeae, the Gorgons' one-eyed sisters, then approached the sleeping Médousa by her reflection in Athena's shield, looking only backward at her (Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2; the scene is already on sixth-century vases). He struck once and lifted the head into the kibisis while her sisters woke — Sthenno and Euryale could not be killed and gave chase, and Perseus escaped on the winged sandals. The beheading encodes the myth's central lesson: Médousa can only be defeated by not being seen, and her own power — reflection — is the weapon that undoes her.

myths.title: The Birth from Blood
myths.text: From Médousa's severed neck sprang two wonders: Pegasus, the immortal winged horse, and Chrysaor, the golden-sworded warrior who would father the three-bodied monster Geryon (Hesiod, Theogony 280–287, 287–294). The arithmetic is startling — the monster's death is the origin of Greek myth's most beautiful creature. Pegasus, tamed by Bellerophon with Athena's bridle, carried the hero against the Chimaira and the Amazons before Bellerophon's fatal attempt on Olympus broke them; the horse ended as Zeus's thunderbolt-bearer, stabled among the stars. Médousa's myth thus runs backward from everyone else's: her catastrophe produces the world's marvels. The blood that dripped to the desert sand, in later tradition, spawned the amphisbaenae and the venomous swarms of Libya — even her wounds generate a bestiary. The Gorgon gives more life in dying than most goddesses give in their whole careers.

myths.title: From Horror to Emblem
myths.text: Perseus gave the head to Athena, who fixed it on her aegis — the Gorgoneion glaring from the goddess's shield (Iliad 5.741), the terror repurposed as armor. From there it became the most traveled apotropaic image in antiquity: on hoplite shields, temple antefixes, city gates, and coins from Paros to Sicily, the round glaring face wards off evil with the monster's own power. Its form migrated too: Archaic art renders the Gorgon as a grinning, tusked, boar-like creature — the great running figure between panthers on the west pediment of the Artemis temple at Corcyra (ca. 580 BCE) — while fifth-century sculptors, in Vernant's famous phrase, 'tamed' the horror into beauty, ending in the classically beautiful severed head. The face that petrified the living became the image that protected the house: the Greeks domesticated terror not by denying it but by mounting it above the door, and calling it theirs.

lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted Médousa directly, and her image proliferated on shields, mosaics, and architectural elements across the empire. Neoplatonists read the petrifying gaze as the material world that must be transcended. Freud made her head the archetype of castration-anxiety and the terror of the female; feminist readings from Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' (1975) onward reclaimed her as the figure of female rage and the male fear of being looked back at — turning Ovid's victim into an avenger. Vernant's La mort dans les yeux (1985) restored her to her proper strangeness: not a symbol of anything, but the face of the look that kills. Her image persists in Caravaggio, in Versace's logo, and in psychology itself, where 'Medusa' names the moment desire turns to stone.
lore.culturalLegacy: Médousa is the most visually recognizable monster in Western art — from the gorgoneia of Archaic temples to Caravaggio's Medusa to Versace's logo, her face sells protection, danger, and luxury in equal measure. Psychologically she is the paralysis of fear, the moment the living turn to stone; in feminist theory she is the emblem of the violence done to women and the rage that answers it, Cixous's banner for women's writing. In film and popular culture she remains the template for every gaze-weapon, from basilisk to comic-book villain. Restoring Médousa restores the name of the figure who turns the gaze back on itself — the guardian, the queen, the mortal one.
lore.extendedMeditation: Médousa is the goddess of the averted gaze. She forces us to look indirectly, to use mirrors and shields, to approach truth without staring directly at it. This is not cowardice; it is wisdom. Some truths petrify. The modern world stares at everything — we believe visibility is virtue and that looking is understanding. Médousa reminds us that some powers are defeated only by indirection, by reflection, by refusing eye contact with horror. And Ovid adds the harder lesson: the face we are forbidden to look at was first a face that was looked at wrongly — by a god in a temple, by a goddess who blamed the victim. The restoration of her name is a small lesson in both visual humility and justice: look carefully at whom your culture has turned to stone.

lore.archaeology: The earliest monumental Gorgon is the running figure of the west pediment of the Temple of Artemis at Corcyra (Corfu, ca. 580 BCE), flanked by panthers. Temples at Selinunte and Athens used gorgoneia as antefixes and akroteria, and Archaic coins from Paros, Neapolis, and Sicily spread the apotropaic type across the Greek world. The Rondanini Medusa (Munich Glyptothek) preserves the late-Classical turn toward beauty, and the beheading scene appears on Attic black- and red-figure vases from the sixth century BCE — archaeology's record of the myth migrating from the world's edge onto every shield and gate.
